title: CloudFormation & CDK
subtitle: Infrastructure as Code — define your entire AWS infrastructure in TypeScript or YAML, version-controlled and reproducible

content.text: Clicking through the AWS console to create resources is fine for learning. In production, it's a liability: no audit trail, hard to reproduce, easy to make mistakes, impossible to diff between environments. Infrastructure as Code (IaC) solves this by describing your infrastructure in code files — versioned in git, reviewed in PRs, automatically applied. Destroying and recreating an entire environment takes minutes, not days.

content.code:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Description: Static website hosting with S3 and CloudFront

Parameters:
  DomainName:
    Type: String
    Description: Domain name for the website
    Default: myapp.com

Resources:
  # S3 bucket for website content
  WebsiteBucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    Properties:
      BucketName: !Sub '${DomainName}-website'
      PublicAccessBlockConfiguration:
        BlockPublicAcls: true
        BlockPublicPolicy: true
        IgnorePublicAcls: true
        RestrictPublicBuckets: true

  # SSL certificate (must be us-east-1 for CloudFront)
  Certificate:
    Type: AWS::CertificateManager::Certificate
    Properties:
      DomainName: !Ref DomainName
      ValidationMethod: DNS

  # CloudFront distribution
  Distribution:
    Type: AWS::CloudFront::Distribution
    Properties:
      DistributionConfig:
        DefaultRootObject: index.html
        Enabled: true
        Origins:
          - Id: S3Origin
            DomainName: !GetAtt WebsiteBucket.RegionalDomainName
        DefaultCacheBehavior:
          TargetOriginId: S3Origin
          ViewerProtocolPolicy: redirect-to-https
          Compress: true
        ViewerCertificate:
          AcmCertificateArn: !Ref Certificate
          SslSupportMethod: sni-only

Outputs:
  DistributionURL:
    Value: !GetAtt Distribution.DomainName
    Description: CloudFront URL

# Deploy:
# aws cloudformation deploy --template-file template.yml --stack-name myapp-website

# Install CDK
npm install -g aws-cdk
npm install aws-cdk-lib constructs

# Bootstrap (one-time per account/region setup)
cdk bootstrap aws://123456789012/us-east-1

# Preview changes (like terraform plan)
cdk diff
# Output: shows what will be created, modified, or deleted

# Deploy
cdk deploy
# Creates/updates the CloudFormation stack

# Destroy all resources
cdk destroy

# Synthesize CloudFormation template (see what CDK generates)
cdk synth

content.text: CDK is CloudFormation with superpowers. CDK compiles to CloudFormation YAML under the hood — cdk synth shows you exactly what CloudFormation template it generates. You get all CloudFormation's reliability and state management, plus the ability to use TypeScript: loops to create multiple similar resources, abstractions (Constructs), type-safe props, and reusable patterns shared as npm packages.

questions.question: You use CloudFormation to create an EC2 instance. You then manually change the instance type in the console. What happens when you run 'cloudformation deploy' again?
options: Nothing — CloudFormation only adds new resources, never modifies existing ones
CloudFormation detects the drift and reverts the instance type back to what the template specifies
CloudFormation fails — it won't deploy if manual changes were detected
CloudFormation ignores the manual change and keeps the console-modified instance type
questions.explanation: CloudFormation uses the template as the source of truth. When you deploy, it compares the desired state (template) to the current state and applies changes to reach the desired state. If you manually changed the instance type from t3.micro to t3.small, the next deploy will change it back to t3.micro. This 'configuration drift' — where reality diverges from the IaC definition — is exactly why IaC enforces consistency. Run 'aws cloudformation detect-stack-drift' to see drifted resources.

faq.q: CDK vs Terraform — which should I learn?
faq.a: Both are excellent. CDK is AWS-only but lets you use TypeScript. Terraform is multi-cloud (AWS, GCP, Azure) with its own HCL language. For AWS-only projects: CDK gives better type safety and access to all new AWS services immediately (no waiting for provider updates). For multi-cloud or existing Terraform organizations: Terraform. Many teams use both: CDK for application infrastructure, Terraform for org-level resources.

examples: Slack manages thousands of AWS resources with CDK. All infrastructure changes go through code review — no one manually clicks in the console. If a region has an outage, they can recreate the entire infrastructure in another region by running 'cdk deploy' with a different region parameter

CDK Constructs are shareable patterns: aws-cdk-lib includes constructs like 'ApplicationLoadBalancedFargateService' that creates an ECS service, task definition, ALB, target group, and security groups in one line of TypeScript
